analysis.one_liner: Requires pharmacy benefit managers to disclose the fees they collect from drug makers and report them publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and its health subcommittee in March 2024, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are the middlemen that negotiate drug coverage for Medicare drug plans and ACA marketplace plans. They collect fees from drug manufacturers, and today only part of that money has to be reported. This bill would require PBMs and their affiliates to disclose every type of fee they receive from manufacturers, how much is passed back to the health plan, and whether plans are being charged a percentage cut, and would have the government publish an annual summary of the data online.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in Medicare prescription drug plans and ACA marketplace plans, who could see through the data how much middlemen and insurers take out of drug spending — information that can be used to push drug prices and premiums down. Health plans themselves also gain negotiating leverage, since they would finally see the full fee picture.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare and ACA drug plan enrollees

how_it_helps.text: Requires PBMs and their affiliates to report the total amount of all fees they receive from drug manufacturers tied to patient use of drugs, broken out by type [S2].
Requires disclosure of the amount and percentage of those manufacturer fees that are actually passed through to the plan, exposing how much the middleman keeps [S2].

Expands reporting to cover the percentage that PBMs take, not just the dollar amount, and covers affiliates that act as price negotiators or group purchasers, closing gaps around the common insurer-PBM ownership structure [S2].
Directs the Health Secretary to publish an annual public report on the CMS website summarizing trends in the reported data, so the numbers are not filed away but visible to the public [S2].

analysis.who_pays: PBMs and their insurer parents (the largest ones are owned by CVS, Cigna, and UnitedHealth), which would bear the cost of detailed fee reporting and lose some of the cover that opaque fee arrangements provide. Drug manufacturers also have new scrutiny of the fees they pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large pharmacy benefit managers and their insurer owners

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates disclosure, not price limits or fee bans; knowing the numbers does not by itself force PBMs to return money to plans or patients, and the reporting applies only to Medicare Part D and ACA plans, not the much larger commercial insurance market [S2].
Compliance costs fall on PBMs and health plans, which may pass some of that cost to premiums, and the effective date is deferred to plan years beginning January 1, 2027 [S2].
The bill drew no cosponsors, so it entered its final Congress with no demonstrated coalition behind it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, low-cost transparency measure aimed at one of the least visible links in the drug-pricing chain. Its benefit is real but indirect: it creates a public paper trail of manufacturer fees rather than directly lowering prices. The honest objection is that sunshine alone moves middlemen slowly, and a first-term bill with zero cosponsors was never positioned to deliver even that outcome.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, then referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee in March and again in December 2024, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on March 19, 2024 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee [S4].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health on March 22, 2024, and referred there again on December 17, 2024 [S4].
No hearing, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred, and the bill attracted no cosponsors [S3].
The bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025; bills that do not pass both chambers before a Congress ends must start over from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large pharmacy benefit managers and their insurer parents, which continue to collect manufacturer fees without the detailed public disclosure this bill would have required, and congressional committees kept discretion over when — or whether — PBM legislation reaches the floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big PBMs and their insurer parents

for.name: Rep. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; it received no cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of first referral; chaired the panel that controls whether PBM bills get a markup
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee in March 2024 and again in December 2024 without ever scheduling a hearing or markup

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Second committee of referral with jurisdiction over Medicare
against.what_they_did: Took the bill's referral but never acted on it during the remaining months of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no organized opposition or support from either party.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: These companies negotiate drug coverage for Medicare and marketplace plans and collect fees from manufacturers whose size is largely hidden today. The bill would force that fee flow into public view, reducing the cover that opacity gives them, though it would not ban any fee.

The biggest PBMs are owned by the largest insurers, so disclosure pressure lands on them too; insurers would also have to report data as health benefits plans. Their PBM subsidiaries' margin depends in part on fees kept from plans, which is what the bill exposes.

Manufacturers pay the fees that would be disclosed, which invites scrutiny of rebate and fee deals, but greater transparency about what PBMs keep can also strengthen manufacturers' negotiating position against the middlemen.
